<ul>
<li><b>Services, carriers, devices.</b> People want services (a warm room, a hot shower, a trip); carriers (gas, electricity, gasoline) bring the energy; devices turn one into the other.</li>
<li><b>Warmth is the biggest home service:</b> 16,900 of the house's 31,100 kWh. The one car uses about as much: 16,900 kWh of gasoline.</li>
<li><b>Swap the furnace for a heat pump:</b> the same 13,500 kWh of heat comes from 5,400 kWh of electricity plus 8,100 kWh moved in from the outdoor air (seasonal COP 2.5). Home and car then buy 36,500 kWh.</li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The heat pump on a cold day (illustrative model)</p>

<thead><tr><th scope="col">Day's outdoor average</th><th scope="col">COP</th><th scope="col">Heat needed</th><th scope="col">Electricity</th></tr></thead>

<tr><td>15 °C</td><td>4.80</td><td>15 kWh</td><td>3 kWh</td></tr>
<tr><td>5 °C</td><td>3.60</td><td>65 kWh</td><td>18 kWh</td></tr>
<tr><td>−5 °C</td><td>2.88</td><td>115 kWh</td><td>40 kWh</td></tr>
<tr><td>−15 °C</td><td>2.40</td><td>165 kWh</td><td>69 kWh</td></tr>
<tr><td>−25 °C (below the −23 °C cut-out: backup heater)</td><td>1.00</td><td>215 kWh</td><td>215 kWh</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you work through this step by step: a tour of the home, a card sort, a guess, the year as a flow diagram, a heat pump swap and a cold day.</p>

The car is the <a href="https://www.epa.gov/energy/greenhouse-gas-equivalencies-calculator-calculations-and-references">EPA's</a> 2022 average: 10,917 miles at 22.8 miles per gallon.<br><b>Illustrative.</b> The furnace (80%), water heater (about 60%) and car (about 30%) efficiencies follow DOE sources listed below. The cold-day heat need and the COP curve are a model, set to pass through DOE's target of COP 2.4 at −15 °C (<a href="https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2021-10/bto-cchp-tech-challenge-spec-102521.pdf">cold-climate heat pump challenge</a>, 2021).</span></p>

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="f3-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Energy service</dt><dd>What people actually want: a warm room, hot water, cold food, light, a trip. The <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-service">service</span> is the goal; energy is the means.</dd>
<dt>Energy carrier</dt><dd>What brings the energy to the home: natural gas, electricity, gasoline. An <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-carrier">energy carrier</span> is bought; a device turns it into the service.</dd>
<dt>Bought and useful</dt><dd>Of 48,000 kWh the home and car buy, 21,700 kWh becomes <span class="lx-term" data-term="useful-energy">useful</span> heat and motion and 17,200 kWh is lost; 9,100 kWh runs appliances and is not split here.</dd>
<dt>Heat pump</dt><dd>It moves heat in from outdoors: in this home 5,400 kWh of electricity plus 8,100 kWh of outdoor heat give the same 13,500 kWh of warmth.</dd>
<dt>Cold days</dt><dd>From a 5 °C day to a −15 °C day the heat need rises 2.5 times, but the electricity 3.8 times, because the COP falls from 3.60 to 2.40.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Primary energy: count the power plant too</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The kWh on a meter are [final energy]{.lx-term term="final-energy"}: what the home buys. Electricity was made somewhere, so its [primary energy]{.lx-term term="primary-energy"} is larger.

Suppose the heat pump's 5,400 kWh came from a gas combined-cycle plant ([F4](f04-power-plants.html): 7,535 Btu of gas per kWh in 2025) through a grid that loses about 5% on the way ([F6](f06-grid-and-outages.html)):

$$
\text{sent out} = \frac{5{,}400 \text{ kWh}}{1 - 0.05} \approx 5{,}700 \text{ kWh}
$$

$$
\text{gas} = 5{,}700 \text{ kWh} \times \frac{7{,}535}{3{,}412} \approx 12{,}600 \text{ kWh}
$$

| Heating the home for a year | Gas burned |
|---|---|
| Gas furnace in the basement | 16,900 kWh |
| Heat pump, its electricity all from that plant | about 12,600 kWh |

That is about 26% less gas, before any wind or solar power enters. Countries count the primary energy of wind, solar and hydro electricity in different ways: F10 (upcoming).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>From services to demand: why cold days are hard to model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A demand model starts from the service and divides by the device's efficiency. For heat on a day with outdoor average $T$ (°C):

| Symbol | Meaning | In this lesson |
|---|---|---|
| $Q(T)$ | heat the home needs that day, kWh | $5 \times \max(0,\, 18 - T)$ (illustrative) |
| $\text{COP}(T)$ | heat delivered ÷ electricity used | $144 / (45 - T)$, so 2.40 at −15 °C |
| $E(T)$ | electricity that day, kWh | $Q(T) / \text{COP}(T)$ |

**Why 144.** An ideal heat pump delivering air at 45 °C could reach the [Carnot limit]{.lx-term term="carnot-limit"}, $T_s / (T_s - T)$ in kelvin: 318.15 ÷ 60 = 5.30 at −15 °C. The model keeps 45% of that ideal, so $0.4526 \times 318.15 = 144$.

**What it means for a model.** $E(T)$ grows faster than $Q(T)$ as $T$ falls, so a model that uses one average temperature underestimates the electricity of the coldest days. Below the −23 °C cut-out it jumps: the backup heater runs at COP 1.

Analyst lesson A15 (upcoming) prices efficiency and electrification; Modeler lesson M12 (upcoming) puts heat, buildings and transport into one city model.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The home mixes averages: each end use is the average of the homes that have it, so no single real home matches it.</li>
<li>Survey estimates are not meters: RECS models each home's end uses from its bills and features.</li>
<li>Useful energy is split only for heat, hot water and the car; cooling, cooking, lighting and devices are left whole.</li>
<li>Equipment efficiencies are single typical values; real ones vary with age, sizing and use.</li>
<li>The cold day uses one daily average temperature, no defrost cycles and no heat-pump capacity limit above the cut-out.</li>
<li>Primary energy here counts only the plant's gas and grid losses, not gas leaks or the energy to drill and pipe it.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 10 minutes: four myths, then four questions.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="f3-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="want" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “What people want is energy.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. People want services: a warm room, a hot shower, a trip. Energy is the means, and different carriers and devices can deliver the same service.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="more" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A heat pump can never deliver more heat than the electricity it uses.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It moves heat from outdoors instead of making it. At a COP of 2.4, DOE's target at −15 °C, 1 kWh of electricity delivers 2.4 kWh of heat.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="fixed" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A heat pump's COP is the same on every day.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Pulling heat from colder air is harder: in this lesson's model the COP falls from 3.60 on a 5 °C day to 2.40 on a −15 °C day.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="car" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Most of the energy in a car's gasoline ends up as heat, not motion.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. About 30% moves a typical gasoline car, depending on the drive (DOE); the rest leaves as waste heat from the engine, exhaust and brakes.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="f3">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="carrier" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which of these is an <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-carrier">energy carrier</span>?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">A warm room</li><li data-value="b">Electricity</li><li data-value="c">A furnace</li><li data-value="d">A hot shower</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Electricity: it brings energy to the home. A warm room and a hot shower are services; a furnace is a device.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="afue" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A furnace with an 80% <span class="lx-term" data-term="afue">AFUE</span> burns gas holding 20,000 kWh in a winter. How much heat reaches the rooms?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">16,000 kWh</li><li data-value="b">20,000 kWh</li><li data-value="c">25,000 kWh</li><li data-value="d">4,000 kWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>16,000 kWh: 20,000 × 0.80. The other 4,000 kWh leaves, mostly up the flue.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cop" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A heat pump with a seasonal <span class="lx-term" data-term="coefficient-of-performance">COP</span> of 2.5 delivers 10,000 kWh of heat in a year. How much electricity does it use?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">25,000 kWh</li><li data-value="b">4,000 kWh</li><li data-value="c">10,000 kWh</li><li data-value="d">7,500 kWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>4,000 kWh: 10,000 ÷ 2.5. The other 6,000 kWh of heat is moved in from the outdoor air.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="snap" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A cold snap doubles a heat-pump home's heat need. Its electricity use…</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">doubles too</li><li data-value="b">less than doubles</li><li data-value="c">more than doubles</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>More than doubles: the heat need doubles and, in colder air, the COP falls, so each kWh of heat takes more electricity.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<ol>
<li><b>Surveys, not meters.</b> EIA's RECS estimates how each surveyed home's energy splits into heating, cooling, hot water and more; most homes have no meter per service.</li>
<li><b>Ratings, not every day.</b> Heat pumps are rated at set test temperatures, such as 5 °F (−15 °C); a real winter brings days above and below them.</li>
<li><b>Where it goes next.</b> Services add up to a town's demand (<a href="02-demand.html">lesson 2</a>) and to the plants that meet it (<a href="f04-power-plants.html">F4</a>).</li>
</ol>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>EIA (2023, revised 2024). <a href="https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2020/index.php?view=consumption">2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey: consumption and expenditures tables</a>. Table CE3.1 (end uses, all homes) and Table CE4.6 (end uses by fuel, averages; West North Central row).</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/units-and-calculators/british-thermal-units.php">Energy explained: British thermal units (Btu)</a>, sample conversion factors (electricity, motor gasoline). Read 3 November 2026.</li>
<li>EPA. <a href="https://www.epa.gov/energy/greenhouse-gas-equivalencies-calculator-calculations-and-references">Greenhouse Gas Equivalencies Calculator: Calculations and References</a>, gasoline-powered passenger vehicles per year (2022 data, from FHWA). Last updated 4 August 2026.</li>
<li>DOE Vehicle Technologies (2024). <a href="https://www.energy.gov/cmei/vehicles/articles/fotw-1360-sept-16-2024-typical-ev-87-91-efficient-compared-30-conventional">FOTW #1360: A Typical EV is 87%–91% Efficient Compared to 30% for a Conventional Gasoline Vehicle</a>. 16 September 2024.</li>
